title: Course
text:
Audience and teaching approach
This course is designed for experienced working professionals. The instructor describes the cohort as having roughly 4–20 years of experience across fields including IT, finance and training. Students bring different kinds of professional expertise; the course does not assume a typical undergraduate background or identical prior knowledge.
The programme is intended to deepen students’ mastery of AI and data science, including agentic AI. Lessons begin with a practical problem before formal definitions. In the first probability lecture, students consider an LLM triage audit of six tickets, including one that requires both Billing and Account Support. Historical interpretations of probability lead to a set-based model for uniformly selecting one ticket ID. The example develops events, their probabilities, and an indicator random variable through its image and inverse image. A separate Gamma model for closure time shows how continuous probabilities are calculated by integration. Worked examples connect calculations to their assumptions and limits. Contexts vary across AI, engineering, IT, finance and training; hypothetical values are identified as such.
For each topic, students identify the quantity or event of interest, examine the available information, calculate under stated assumptions, and then study the formal definition. Lessons include many short, tractable problems with worked solutions so students can build fluency at a measured pace. Course prose is factual and formal, without aphorisms or dramatic framing.

text:
2. Historical development and interpretations
Problems of chance helped drive the development of probability: Pascal and Fermat’s correspondence in 1654 examined how to reason about uncertain outcomes in games. The translated correspondence shows the role of concrete problems. Later interpretations emphasized equal-likelihood counting, repeated observations, belief and evidential support. These remain different ways of understanding an assignment of probability, rather than a sequence in which each simply replaced the previous one.
Kolmogorov’s 1933 axiomatic foundation supplied a common mathematical framework for probability calculations; see the historical introduction in Imperial College’s probability notes. It specifies the rules a probability model must obey. It does not, by itself, choose the appropriate sampling mechanism or probability assignment for an application. We first compare interpretations using the audit, then use Bertrand’s question to see why a model needs to be specified.
Probability has been interpreted in several ways. The accounts below answer different questions about what the number 4/64/6 might mean. None follows just from seeing six rows in a table.

Classical equal-likelihood
The classical rule counts favourable outcomes among equally likely cases. If one ticket ID is selected uniformly from the six IDs, four selections produce agreement, so
P(agreement)=46=23.P(\text{agreement})=\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.
This calculation is valid for that selection experiment. It does not imply that future tickets are equally likely to be any of these six records, or that the six records represent future traffic. A finite list defines possible cases; the uniform selection rule supplies the equal weights.
The partition chosen for counting also matters. Group the tickets by the pair (reviewer outcome, model classification):

There are four occupied pair types in this audit. If an experiment selected one of these four types uniformly, two of the four would be exact matches, giving 2/42/4. If it selected one of the six ticket IDs uniformly, the pair types would instead have probabilities 1/6,2/6,2/6,1/61/6,2/6,2/6,1/6, giving 4/64/6. Thresholding two destination scores separately permits four model outputs: neither, Billing only, Account Support only, or both. Thus the full product contains 4×4=164\times4=16 reviewer/model pairs, of which four occur in this audit. Uniform selection among all 16 pairs would be a third experiment; its four matching pairs would give agreement probability 4/16=1/44/16=1/4. Equal weighting of pair types does not follow from grouping tickets that way. Counting requires a stated set of cases and a reason to treat those cases as equally likely.


Frequency
The observed agreement proportion is
p̂6=16∑i=16Ii=46,\widehat p_6=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{i=1}^{6}I_i=\frac{4}{6},
where Ii=1I_i=1 when the model classification exactly matches the reviewer’s reference outcome for ticket tit_i, and Ii=0I_i=0 otherwise. A frequency interpretation connects a probability to the limiting relative frequency in a specified repeatable process. This audit records one finite set of six tickets; it does not establish that limit or show that future ticket mix and model performance will remain the same.
Repeatedly sampling the LLM for the same text under randomized decoding would define another process. Its output frequency would describe generated classifications, not necessarily agreement with reviewer decisions. The process and event must be stated before interpreting a frequency.


Subjective probability and Bayesian updating
A subjective interpretation treats probability as a person’s degree of belief given available information. An analyst might assess the chance that the model agrees with the review protocol on a future ticket, using this audit and other stated information. The six rows do not determine that assessment uniquely. Coherence constrains probability assignments; subjective does not mean arbitrary. Countable additivity is an additional condition in the Kolmogorov model and does not follow from every finite coherence argument.
Bayesian updating describes how an assessment changes when evidence is observed. If HH is the proposition that the next ticket’s model classification will agree with its reference outcome and DD is additional evidence, Bayes’ rule gives
P(H∣D)=P(D∣H)P(H)P(D),P(D)>0.P(H\mid D)=\frac{P(D\mid H)P(H)}{P(D)},\qquad P(D)>0.
The formula does not supply the prior or likelihood; those come from a model and stated information. Conditional probability and Bayesian updating will be developed later.


Logical or evidential probability
A logical or evidential interpretation aims to quantify how strongly stated evidence supports a proposition. Here the evidence could include the six audit rows, the review protocol and assumptions about the future ticket population. A numerical answer requires a rule connecting that evidence and those assumptions to a degree of support. If the rule invokes indifference, it must specify which cases are treated equally and why. Counting ticket IDs and counting occupied label-pair types give different answers because they describe different selection rules. This identifies a problem with an unspecified indifference rule; it does not refute every logical account.


What the interpretations leave for a probability model
Classical probability emphasizes equal likelihood, frequency emphasizes repetition, subjective probability represents an assessment given information, and logical accounts specify evidential support. A propensity account would treat the configured randomized generation process as the chance-producing mechanism. These accounts differ in interpretation. A mathematical calculation also needs the possible outcomes, the event of interest and a probability assignment. The next example shows why the sampling procedure is part of that specification.
Checkpoint 2. For each interpretation, state what additional assumption or information is needed to use it for a claim about future tickets.

section: 3. A second question: Bertrand’s random chord
text:
3. A second question: Bertrand’s random chord
Draw an equilateral triangle inside a circle. Consider the question:

If a chord is selected at random from the circle, what is the probability that its length exceeds the side length of the triangle?

The phrase “selected at random” does not specify how the chord is generated. Bertrand described different sampling procedures for chords, which give 1/31/3, 1/21/2 and 1/41/4 for the same length comparison. These values follow from different probability distributions induced by the respective sampling procedures; the problem statement alone does not say which procedure to use. John D. Norton’s University of Pittsburgh page presents the three sampling arguments and their values.
The procedures are: choose two independent uniform endpoints (1/31/3); choose a uniform radial distance and an independent uniform direction (1/21/2); or choose a midpoint uniformly in disk area (1/41/4). These are different models. We will not choose among them or derive the answers in this section. The example identifies information a probability question can leave unspecified: the outcomes and, especially, the sampling rule that determines their probabilities.

Kolmogorov’s set-based framework
Kolmogorov’s axiomatic framework gives probability a mathematical foundation in terms of sets and a measure. Its three objects are written
(Ω,ℱ,P).(\Omega,\mathcal F,P).
Here Ω\Omega is the sample space of possible outcomes, ℱ\mathcal F is the collection of events to which probabilities are assigned, and P:ℱ→[0,1]P:\mathcal F\to[0,1] is the probability measure. The measure obeys nonnegativity, normalization and countable additivity. We will understand these rules through the ticket audit. Section 5 explains the event-collection requirements in a definition box; their further development belongs to the supplement. The supplement returns to Bertrand’s question and specifies the sampling models in full.

4. Define the experiment and its events
To calculate a probability for the audit, specify an experiment:

Select one of the six ticket IDs uniformly at random.

The ticket records, reviewer decisions and model classifications are fixed. The selected ticket ID is the outcome that varies. Thus the sample space is
Ω={t1,t2,t3,t4,t5,t6}.\Omega=\{t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4,t_5,t_6\}.
The sample space is the set of possible outcomes; exactly one outcome occurs in a selection. An event is a set of outcomes satisfying a condition. It occurs when the selected outcome belongs to that set.
Define events from the reviewer’s reference classification:
B={t1,t2,t5},A={t1,t3,t6},B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\},\qquad
A=\{t_1,t_3,t_6\},

O=(B∪A)c={t4}.O=(B\cup A)^c=\{t_4\}.
In this model, OO is precisely the “Other” reference outcome. It is disjoint from BB and AA. The ticket t1t_1 belongs to both BB and AA, because both destinations are required:

=\frac{3}{6}+\frac{3}{6}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{5}{6}.
The complement is OO, so P(O)=1/6P(O)=1/6. The reviewer outcomes form four possible destination sets: both, Billing only, Account Support only, or neither. “Other” refers only to the last of these in this example.

text:
5. From a calculation to the triplet and axioms
In the audit, selecting Billing-only, Account-only, both, or neither has probabilities 2/6,2/6,1/6,1/62/6,2/6,1/6,1/6. These four categories do not overlap and cover every ticket, so their probabilities add to 1. No category has a negative probability. These observations motivate the rules for a probability model.
The experiment is represented by the probability triplet
(Ω,ℱ,P).(\Omega,\mathcal F,P).








Object
Ticket-audit model
Meaning




Ω\Omega
{t1,t2,t3,t4,t5,t6}\{t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4,t_5,t_6\}
Possible outcomes: ticket IDs that may be selected


ℱ\mathcal F
2Ω2^\Omega
Events: all subsets of the six ticket IDs


PP
P(E)=|E|/6P(E)=|E|/6 for E⊆ΩE\subseteq\Omega
Probability measure under uniform selection



An outcome such as t2t_2 is an element of Ω\Omega. An event such as BB is a subset of Ω\Omega. The measure PP takes an event as input and returns a number in [0,1][0,1]. Here the uniform rule assigns probability 1/61/6 to each singleton outcome.






NoteDefinition: power set — the collection of all subsets



For a sample space Ω\Omega, its power set is
2Ω=𝒫(Ω)={E:E⊆Ω}.2^\Omega=\mathcal P(\Omega)=\{E:E\subseteq\Omega\}.
It is a set whose members are themselves sets. For Ω={a,b,c}\Omega=\{a,b,c\}, the full list is
𝒫(Ω)={⌀,{a},{b},{c},{a,b},{a,c},{b,c},{a,b,c}}.\mathcal P(\Omega)=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\{c\},
\{a,b\},\{a,c\},\{b,c\},\{a,b,c\}\}.
Here a∈Ωa\in\Omega, {a}⊆Ω\{a\}\subseteq\Omega, and {a}∈𝒫(Ω)\{a\}\in\mathcal P(\Omega) are different statements. The empty set is the impossible event; Ω\Omega is the certain event. If Ω\Omega has nn elements, its power set has 2n2^n members: each element can be included or excluded from a subset. The six-ticket space therefore has 64 possible events, not 64 outcomes.


Choosing all subsets as events is convenient for our finite models. It allows questions about individual tickets as well as groups. This choice says nothing about whether their probabilities are equal.
Suppose instead that a dashboard on {a,b,c}\{a,b,c\} reports only “one of a,ba,b” or “cc.” It can answer the event {a,b}\{a,b\} and its opposite {c}\{c\}, together with the certain and impossible events. It cannot distinguish aa from bb. This motivates specifying which collection of events the model uses.






NoteDefinition: sigma-algebra — a collection of events closed under logical combinations



A sigma-algebra ℱ\mathcal F on Ω\Omega is a collection of subsets of Ω\Omega satisfying:

Ω∈ℱ\Omega\in\mathcal F: the certain event is available.
If E∈ℱE\in\mathcal F, then Ec=Ω\E∈ℱE^c=\Omega\setminus E\in\mathcal F: if a question is available, “not that event” is available.
If E1,E2,…∈ℱE_1,E_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F, then ⋃n=1∞En∈ℱ\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\in\mathcal F: “at least one occurs” is available for a countable list of events.

Closed means that performing the stated operation keeps us inside the same collection. Countable means finite or listable as E1,E2,…E_1,E_2,\ldots; it does not mean an arbitrary collection of any size. The events in a union need not be disjoint for the union to belong to ℱ\mathcal F.
These requirements concern which sets are events, not the numerical probabilities assigned to them. In the triplet (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), ℱ\mathcal F supplies the events and PP assigns their probabilities.








TipWorked check: a full collection and a smaller collection



Every power set 𝒫(Ω)\mathcal P(\Omega) is a sigma-algebra: the whole space, complements and unions of subsets of Ω\Omega are still subsets of Ω\Omega.
For the dashboard, 𝒢={⌀,{a,b},{c},Ω}\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\{a,b\},\{c\},\Omega\} is also a sigma-algebra. Complements exchange the two nontrivial groups, and every union is again one of the four listed sets. In particular, a countable union still combines only these four distinct sets. The set {a}\{a\} is a subset of Ω\Omega but is not an event in this smaller model.
By contrast, {⌀,Ω,{a}}\{\varnothing,\Omega,\{a\}\} is not a sigma-algebra on {a,b,c}\{a,b,c\}: it omits the required complement {b,c}\{b,c\}.








NoteUseful properties of a sigma-algebra



The three requirements imply:

⌀∈ℱ\varnothing\in\mathcal F, since ⌀=Ωc\varnothing=\Omega^c.
Countable intersections are events: “all occur” can be written as “not at least one fails,” ⋂nEn=(⋃nEnc)c.\bigcap_n E_n=\left(\bigcup_n E_n^c\right)^c.
Differences are events: E\F=E∩FcE\setminus F=E\cap F^c means “EE occurs and FF does not.”
Finite unions and intersections are included as special cases.

A sigma-algebra need not be the full power set. In continuous models we use an appropriate event collection containing intervals and their usual combinations; the supplement explains Borel sets and why further care is needed.








ImportantKolmogorov’s axioms — rules for the probability assignment



On the event collection ℱ\mathcal F, the probability measure PP satisfies:

Nonnegativity: P(E)≥0P(E)\ge0 for every event EE.
Normalization: P(Ω)=1P(\Omega)=1.
Countable additivity: for pairwise disjoint events E1,E2,…E_1,E_2,\ldots, P(⋃n=1∞En)=∑n=1∞P(En).P\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\right)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(E_n).

Pairwise disjoint means Ei∩Ej=⌀E_i\cap E_j=\varnothing whenever i≠ji\ne j. In this case there is no overlap to count twice. Unlike closure of a sigma-algebra under unions, adding probabilities without a correction requires disjointness.
The axioms do not say that outcomes are equally likely. Uniform and nonuniform assignments can both satisfy them.


For the six singleton events, additivity gives P(Ω)=6(1/6)=1P(\Omega)=6(1/6)=1. Also BB and BcB^c are disjoint and exhaustive, and P(B)+P(Bc)=3/6+3/6=1P(B)+P(B^c)=3/6+3/6=1. The same addition rule applies to any countable list of disjoint events; on this six-outcome space, only finitely many can be nonempty.
A probability measure is a set function: it takes an event as input and returns a number between 0 and 1. The event BB is a set of tickets; P(B)=1/2P(B)=1/2 is a number. This keeps the sample point, event and probability value distinct.

6. Record a number: random variables and distributions
Suppose the audit spreadsheet needs a 1 when Billing is required and a 0 otherwise. Selecting a ticket uniformly produces the entries 1,1,0,0,1,01,1,0,0,1,0 on the six possible rows. Three rows give 1, so the probability of recording 1 is 3/6=1/23/6=1/2.
A random variable assigns a numerical value to each outcome. For this experiment define the Billing indicator
XB:Ω→ℝ,XB(t)={1,t∈B,0,t∉B.X_B:\Omega\to\mathbb R,\qquad
X_B(t)=\begin{cases}
1,&t\in B,\\
0,&t\notin B.
\end{cases}
Its values are
XB(t1)=1,XB(t2)=1,XB(t3)=0,XB(t4)=0,XB(t5)=1,XB(t6)=0.X_B(t_1)=1,\;X_B(t_2)=1,\;X_B(t_3)=0,\;X_B(t_4)=0,
\;X_B(t_5)=1,\;X_B(t_6)=0.
Write X:Ω→ℝX:\Omega\to\mathbb R for a real-valued random variable. Once the outcome is known, its value is fixed. Here the selection of a ticket is random; the rule for recording Billing is fixed.
The inputs distinguish two functions: XBX_B takes one ticket and returns 0 or 1; PP takes a set of tickets and returns its probability. Thus PP is called a set function. The term describes the type of input. Having a set as its domain does not make every function a set function. The supplement gives the technical condition for random variables in general probability spaces.

Image: values produced by a set of outcomes
For E⊆ΩE\subseteq\Omega, the image of EE under XBX_B is
XB(E)={XB(t):t∈E}.X_B(E)=\{X_B(t):t\in E\}.
For the Account Support event A={t1,t3,t6}A=\{t_1,t_3,t_6\}, t1t_1 also requires Billing, while t3t_3 and t6t_6 do not. Hence
XB(A)={0,1}.X_B(A)=\{0,1\}.
This is a set of numerical values, not an event in the ticket sample space.


Inverse image: outcomes that produce selected values
For D⊆ℝD\subseteq\mathbb R, the inverse image is
XB−1(D)={t∈Ω:XB(t)∈D}.X_B^{-1}(D)=\{t\in\Omega:X_B(t)\in D\}.
In particular,
XB−1({1})={t1,t2,t5}=B,X_B^{-1}(\{1\})=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\}=B,
and
XB−1({0})={t3,t4,t6}=Bc.X_B^{-1}(\{0\})=\{t_3,t_4,t_6\}=B^c.
An inverse image is a set of outcomes; it need not be an inverse function. The inverse image connects a numerical condition on a random variable to an event to which the probability measure applies:
P(XB=1)=P(XB−1({1}))=P(B)=36=12.P(X_B=1)=P\bigl(X_B^{-1}(\{1\})\bigr)=P(B)=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12.
The distribution of XBX_B is P(XB=1)=1/2P(X_B=1)=1/2 and P(XB=0)=1/2P(X_B=0)=1/2. The function XBX_B, its inverse-image event BB, and the number P(B)P(B) are three different objects.

7. A continuous measurement: probability as area
A stipulated sensor model has error ε\varepsilon uniformly distributed between −2-2 and 22 mm. What is the probability that the error is between −0.5-0.5 and 0.50.5 mm?
Uniformity assigns probabilities in proportion to interval length. The favorable interval has length 1 mm, while the full interval has length 4 mm. Therefore
P(−0.5≤ε≤0.5)=14.P(-0.5\le\varepsilon\le0.5)=\frac{1}{4}.
We describe this with a probability density f(e)=1/4f(e)=1/4 per mm on [−2,2][-2,2], and zero elsewhere. The rectangle above an interval has area equal to its probability. Its total area is 4(1/4)=14(1/4)=1. More generally, a density is nonnegative, has total area 1, and gives interval probabilities by
P(a≤X≤b)=∫abf(x)dx.P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.
A density height is not a probability. Under this continuous model, an exact point has probability zero, although a measured error must have some value. Recorded, rounded measurements describe intervals rather than infinitely precise points. Not every random variable has a density: the head count in Section 6 has discrete probabilities.
The sample space here is [−2,2][-2,2]; the events used in these calculations are intervals and combinations of intervals; the probability measure assigns their lengths divided by 4. The precise event collection is developed in the unit-interval example in the supplement. Uniform error is an assumption for teaching, not a consequence of a manufacturer’s tolerance limit. A more involved closure-time density is also worked out in the supplement.

8. Worked problems across domains

Worked example 1: probability of “Other”
Find the probability that a uniformly selected ticket has neither Billing nor Account Support required according to the reviewer.
Solution. By definition, O=(B∪A)c={t4}O=(B\cup A)^c=\{t_4\}. Therefore
P(O)=16.P(O)=\frac{1}{6}.


Worked example 2: exactly one named destination is required
Find the event and probability that exactly one of Billing and Account Support is required.
Solution. The event is
(B\A)∪(A\B)={t2,t3,t5,t6}. (B\setminus A)\cup(A\setminus B)=\{t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\}.
Its probability is 4/6=2/34/6=2/3.


Worked example 3: agreement between reviewer and model
Let M(t)M(t) be the model’s classification and R(t)R(t) the reviewer’s reference classification for ticket tt. Define exact agreement as equality of these classification sets. The agreement event from the table is
C={t2,t3,t5,t6}.C=\{t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6\}.
Under uniform selection, P(C)=4/6=2/3P(C)=4/6=2/3. This equals the observed agreement fraction because the experiment selects uniformly from this exact audit.


Worked example 4: record agreement numerically
Define Y(t)=1Y(t)=1 if the model classification exactly matches the reviewer and Y(t)=0Y(t)=0 otherwise. Then Y−1({1})=CY^{-1}(\{1\})=C, and
P(Y=1)=P(C)=46=23.P(Y=1)=P(C)=\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.
The random variable records an outcome numerically; its inverse image gives the event; the probability measure assigns that event a number.


Worked example 5: change the audit selection weights
In a hypothetical follow-up experiment, select the same six IDs with stipulated weights (1,1,1,3,1,1)/8(1,1,1,3,1,1)/8. Keep Ω\Omega, its full power set and the labels fixed. Find the probabilities of agreement and Other.
Solution. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one, defining Q(E)=∑ti∈EwiQ(E)=\sum_{t_i\in E}w_i. Therefore Q(C)=(1+1+1+1)/8=1/2Q(C)=(1+1+1+1)/8=1/2 and Q(O)=3/8Q(O)=3/8. The observed fraction remains 4/64/6, but the selection probability changes. These weights specify an exercise, not an estimate of future traffic.


Worked example 6: fraud-screen flags
A hypothetical fixed review batch has 20 transaction IDs. Reviewers label 4 as fraudulent. A screen flags 5: 3 of the 4 reviewer-positive transactions and 2 reviewer-negative transactions. Select one ID uniformly. Find the false-positive and false-negative events’ probabilities.
Solution. On Ω={1,…,20}\Omega=\{1,\ldots,20\} with its power set and uniform measure, write FF for flagged IDs and HH for reviewer-positive IDs. Then |F∩Hc|=2|F\cap H^c|=2 and |Fc∩H|=1|F^c\cap H|=1, so their probabilities are 2/20=0.102/20=0.10 and 1/20=0.051/20=0.05. Among the 16 reviewer-negative records, the false-positive fraction is instead 2/16=0.1252/16=0.125. That changes the denominator and the selection experiment; it is not the probability just calculated.


Worked example 7: sensor tolerance
For a hypothetical engineering model, a sensor error ε\varepsilon is uniform on [−2,2][-2,2] millimetres. Use this interval as the sample space and density f(e)=1/4f(e)=1/4 on the interval. What is the probability of exceeding a tolerance of 1 mm in absolute value?
Solution. The failure event is [−2,−1)∪(1,2][-2,-1)\cup(1,2], of total length 2, giving P(|ε|>1)=∫[−2,−1)∪(1,2](1/4)de=1/2P(|\varepsilon|>1)=\int_{[-2,-1)\cup(1,2]}(1/4)de=1/2. Exact boundary values have probability zero under this model. Uniform error is stipulated, not established by the tolerance specification.


Worked example 8: assessment pass indicator
Select one of five hypothetical assessment records uniformly. Their fixed scores are 45, 60, 70, 80 and 95; the pass threshold is 60 inclusive. Specify a random variable and its law for the pass/fail result.
Solution. Outcomes are record IDs a1,…,a5a_1,\ldots,a_5, with the power set and singleton weights 1/51/5. Set Y(ai)=𝟏{score(ai)≥60}Y(a_i)=\mathbf1_{\{\text{score}(a_i)\ge60\}}. Then Y−1({1})={a2,a3,a4,a5}Y^{-1}(\{1\})=\{a_2,a_3,a_4,a_5\}, PY({1})=4/5P_Y(\{1\})=4/5 and PY({0})=1/5P_Y(\{0\})=1/5. This is a probability under selection from these records; it does not establish a future cohort’s pass rate.


Worked example 9: Electrical engineering: two power supplies
A hypothetical device has a primary and a backup supply. The stipulated probabilities for (primary, backup) are (W,W):0.90(W,W):0.90, (W,F):0.06(W,F):0.06, (F,W):0.03(F,W):0.03, (F,F):0.01(F,F):0.01, where WW means working and FF means failed. The device operates if at least one supply works. Find its operating probability.
Working. The four states are the outcomes; all their subsets are events. Their probabilities are nonnegative and sum to 1. The device fails only in (F,F)(F,F), so P(operates)=1−0.01=0.99P(\text{operates})=1-0.01=0.99. Direct addition gives 0.90+0.06+0.03=0.990.90+0.06+0.03=0.99. This introduces the complement rule P(Ec)=1−P(E)P(E^c)=1-P(E). The joint state probabilities are given; independence of the supplies is not assumed.


Worked example 10: IT operations: overlapping incident tags
Select uniformly one of 40 fixed incident IDs in a hypothetical log. Twelve have a network tag, nine a storage tag, and four have both. Find the probabilities of at least one tag, exactly one tag, and neither tag.
Working. Let NN and SS be the two tagged sets. At least one contains 12+9−4=1712+9-4=17 IDs, so its probability is 17/4017/40. Exactly one contains (12−4)+(9−4)=13(12-4)+(9-4)=13 IDs, giving 13/4013/40. Neither contains 40−17=2340-17=23 IDs, giving 23/4023/40. Tags can overlap even though only one incident ID is selected.


Worked example 11: Accounting: reconciliation categories
A hypothetical ledger has 30 distinct invoice IDs: 21 reconcile correctly, 5 have only a missing receipt, 3 have only an amount mismatch, and 1 has both issues. Select one ID uniformly. Find the probabilities of any issue and of an amount mismatch.
Working. The four disjoint categories have probabilities 21/30,5/30,3/30,1/3021/30,5/30,3/30,1/30, which sum to 1. Any issue has probability (5+3+1)/30=9/30(5+3+1)/30=9/30. An amount mismatch includes the last two categories, so its probability is (3+1)/30=4/30(3+1)/30=4/30. Category names must specify whether overlapping issues are included.


Worked example 12: Agriculture: plot selection and area selection
A hypothetical farm has plot A of area 1 hectare and plot B of area 3 hectares. All of A is classified as stressed and none of B is. First select a plot ID uniformly and report its classification. Then consider selecting a location uniformly by area across the farm. Find the probability of reporting stress in each experiment.
Working. For uniform plot selection, Ω={A,B}\Omega=\{A,B\} and P({A})=1/2P(\{A\})=1/2. For uniform area selection, the stressed area is 1 out of 4 hectares, giving probability 1/41/4. At the plot-label level the second experiment assigns weights 1/41/4 and 3/43/4. Changing the sampling unit changes the probability. Neither answer estimates an unstated future drought risk.


Worked example 13: Finance: a loss distribution from fixed records
Select one of ten hypothetical contract records uniformly. Six have a recorded loss of ₹0, three have ₹100, and one has ₹500. Let LL record the loss. Find its distribution, P(L>0)P(L>0) and P(L≥100)P(L\ge100).
Working. The outcomes are the ten contract IDs, while LL takes values 0, 100 and 500. Counting the IDs gives P(L=0)=6/10P(L=0)=6/10, P(L=100)=3/10P(L=100)=3/10, and P(L=500)=1/10P(L=500)=1/10. Thus P(L>0)=4/10P(L>0)=4/10 and P(L≥100)=4/10P(L\ge100)=4/10. The events coincide on these records. Three loss values do not receive equal probabilities. This describes selection from a fixed ledger, not a forecast.


Worked example 14: Support: number of required destinations
For the six-ticket audit, record D(t)D(t), the number of named destinations required by the reviewer: Billing and Account Support. Find the distribution of DD under uniform ticket selection.
Working. Ticket t4t_4 gives 0, tickets t2,t3,t5,t6t_2,t_3,t_5,t_6 give 1, and t1t_1 gives 2. Hence P(D=0)=1/6P(D=0)=1/6, P(D=1)=4/6P(D=1)=4/6 and P(D=2)=1/6P(D=2)=1/6. The probabilities sum to 1. “Other” means zero of these two named destinations, not that no support is needed.


Worked example 15: Agriculture: germination counts
Select one of eight hypothetical seed-tray records uniformly. The recorded numbers of germinated seeds are 0,1,1,2,2,2,3,30,1,1,2,2,2,3,3. Let GG be the recorded count. Find its distribution and the probability of at least two germinated seeds.
Working. Tray IDs are equally likely; their counts are not. The distribution is P(G=0)=1/8P(G=0)=1/8, P(G=1)=2/8P(G=1)=2/8, P(G=2)=3/8P(G=2)=3/8, P(G=3)=2/8P(G=3)=2/8. Therefore P(G≥2)=(3+2)/8=5/8P(G\ge2)=(3+2)/8=5/8. No assumption of independent seed germination is needed to describe selection from these fixed records.


Worked example 16: IT monitoring: a continuous waiting time
A monitoring check runs every 10 minutes. Stipulate that an incident arrives at a uniformly distributed time within one checking cycle. Let WW be the wait until the next check. What is P(W>7)P(W>7)?
Working. The waiting time is uniform on [0,10][0,10] minutes. Waiting more than 7 minutes occupies an interval of length 3, so P(W>7)=3/10P(W>7)=3/10. Equivalently, the density is 1/101/10 per minute and the area is 3(1/10)3(1/10). A periodic checking schedule alone does not establish the uniform arrival assumption.


Practice with equally likely outcomes
For each exercise below, first specify the elementary outcomes and the sampling assumptions. Use the finite triplet
(Ω,2Ω,P),P({ω})=1|Ω|,P(E)=|E||Ω|.\left(\Omega,2^\Omega,P\right),\qquad P(\{\omega\})=\frac1{|\Omega|},\qquad P(E)=\frac{|E|}{|\Omega|}.
The stated mechanisms make the elementary toss sequences, ordered die pairs, individual cards, ordered draws or selected subsets equiprobable. Records and summaries computed from those outcomes need not be equally likely. Fairness and independence are stipulated for coins and dice; uniform selection is stipulated for cards and people.
For successive uniform draws of two distinct objects from nn objects, use the rule that each ordered pair has probability 1/[n(n−1)]1/[n(n-1)]. We stipulate this rule here; its product form (1/n)(1/(n−1))(1/n)(1/(n-1)) will be justified using conditional probability. These practice questions have no worked answers in the student materials.
When a selection has no order, (nk)\binom nk denotes the number of kk-element subsets of nn distinct objects. In particular, (n2)=n(n−1)/2\binom n2=n(n-1)/2; justify the factor of 2 when comparing ordered roles with committees in P3.

Coins
C1. Two tosses and overlapping events. Toss a fair coin twice independently. Let EE be “the first toss is heads” and FF be “exactly one head.” List Ω,E,F,E∩F\Omega,E,F,E\cap F and E∪FE\cup F, and calculate their event probabilities. Are EE and FF mutually exclusive?
C2. Three tosses. Toss a fair coin three times independently. Find the probabilities of exactly two heads, at least two heads, and at least one head. Calculate the last probability both by counting directly and by using the complement.
C3. From sequences to a random variable. For the same three-toss experiment, define N(ω)N(\omega) as the number of heads. List N−1({k})N^{-1}(\{k\}) for k=0,1,2,3k=0,1,2,3 and give the law of NN. Explain why assigning probability 1/41/4 to each possible head count would describe a different model.


Dice
D1. One die. Roll one stipulated fair six-sided die. Let EE be “an even face” and FF be “a face greater than 3.” List their intersection and union. Find P(E∪F)P(E\cup F) and the probability of exactly one of E,FE,F occurring.
D2. Two distinguishable dice. Roll independent fair red and blue six-sided dice. Use ordered pairs (r,b)(r,b) as outcomes. Find the probabilities of a total of 7, a double, and a total of at least 10. Show the favorable pairs or their counts.
D3. Forgetting the colours. Keep D2’s experiment, but record S(r,b)=(min⁡(r,b),max⁡(r,b))S(r,b)=(\min(r,b),\max(r,b)), the two faces in increasing order, allowing equality. How many possible records are there? Are these records equally likely? Find P(S=(1,1))P(S=(1,1)) and P(S=(1,2))P(S=(1,2)) by counting their preimages in the original 36-outcome space, then calculate the probability of recording at least one 1.


A deck of cards
Use a standard deck of 52 distinct cards with no jokers: 13 ranks in each of four suits, with one ace per suit. In each draw, choose uniformly from the cards currently available. In K2 and K3 the two cards are drawn without replacement.
K1. One card and a union. Specify the sample space using card identities. Find the probability that the card is an ace or a heart. Explain why adding 4/524/52 and 13/5213/52 without correction is wrong.
K2. Two ordered draws. Record the first and second cards separately. How many elementary outcomes are there, and why are they equally likely? Find the probabilities that both cards are aces and that the first is an ace while the second is not.
K3. An unordered two-card hand. Select a two-card subset uniformly. Find the probability of exactly one ace. Recalculate it using ordered draws without replacement and verify agreement. Explain why “zero aces”, “one ace” and “two aces” are not three equiprobable outcomes.


Selecting people
In a hypothetical training group, six distinct participants have IDs a,b,c,d,e,fa,b,c,d,e,f. Four, a,b,c,da,b,c,d, have completed a specified training module; e,fe,f have not. These are fixed labels. Every selection below follows the stated uniform mechanism.
P1. One participant. Select one of the six IDs uniformly. Find the probability that the selected participant has completed the module and the probability that the selected ID is aa or ff. Distinguish an individual outcome from the event “completed.”
P2. A two-person committee. Select a two-element subset uniformly from the six participants. Find the probabilities that both have completed the module, exactly one has completed it, and neither has completed it. Check that these probabilities sum to 1. Why should the denominator count committees rather than completion categories?
P3. Two distinct roles. Select a chair uniformly from all six participants, then a secretary uniformly from the remaining five. Use ordered pairs of distinct IDs. Find the probabilities that the chair has completed the module and the secretary has not, and that the two office holders are aa and bb in either order. If the role labels are discarded, is the resulting committee uniform over the 15 pairs? Justify your answer by counting preimages.


Reflection

Which assumptions establish equiprobability in each experiment?
Does uniform sampling of elementary outcomes make head counts, dice totals or committee compositions uniform? Explain using an exercise above.
When does discarding order preserve uniformity? Compare dice records, two-card hands and two-person committees.
A hypothetical evaluation set has 8 cases of one task type and 2 of another. Under uniform selection of a case ID, are the two task types equally likely? Instead choose either task type with probability 1/21/2, then select a case uniformly within that type. Find the probabilities of each type and of each individual case under this second rule.




Practice across domains
All scenarios below are hypothetical. For finite experiments, specify the outcome IDs, use all subsets as events and state the selection weights before calculating.
A1. Electrical inspection. Select one of 50 hypothetical circuit-board IDs uniformly. Eight fail a voltage test, six fail a current test, and three fail both. Find the probabilities of failing at least one test, failing exactly one, and passing both.
A2. IT latency records. Select uniformly one of eight hypothetical request IDs whose recorded latencies in milliseconds are 40,40,50,50,50,80,100,15040,40,50,50,50,80,100,150. Define XX as latency. Give its distribution and find P(X>80)P(X>80) and P(X≥80)P(X\ge80).
A3. Accounting audit. A hypothetical ledger has 24 invoice IDs. Six lack approval, five lack a receipt, and two lack both. Select one ID uniformly. Find the probability of neither issue. Define an indicator for at least one issue and give its distribution.
A4. Agricultural sampling. Three hypothetical plots have areas 1, 2 and 5 hectares. Only the third plot is classified as stressed throughout. Compare the probability of reporting stress under uniform plot-ID selection and uniform location selection by area. Specify the weights on the three plot labels in each model.
A5. Finance records. Select one of twelve hypothetical loan IDs uniformly. Eight have recorded loss ₹0, three have ₹200 and one has ₹1000. Define a loss random variable, give its distribution and find the probability of a loss strictly greater than ₹200.
A6. Support selection weights. Three hypothetical queues contain 2, 3 and 5 fixed ticket IDs. Either select one of all ten IDs uniformly, or choose a queue uniformly and then an ID uniformly within it. Find the probability of each queue and of each individual ticket under both rules.
A7. Continuous measurement. Stipulate a uniformly distributed voltage error on [−0.2,0.2][-0.2,0.2] volts. Find the probability of absolute error greater than 0.05 volts, and the probability of an error exactly equal to 0.05 volts. Explain the units of the density.

9. Connection to AI evaluation and continuation
The probability 2/32/3 here concerns uniform selection from six audited ticket IDs. It is not automatically the model’s agreement probability on future traffic. That requires a defined target population, an appropriate sampling process and assumptions connecting this audit to future tickets. Changing the reviewer protocol may also change the event called “agreement.”
The same distinctions arise in AI evaluation. A test-set accuracy is an observed proportion. Interpreting it as a probability of correct classification for future cases requires additional assumptions. If model generation is stochastic, its repeated-output distribution is another probability model with a different outcome space. In each case, specify the outcomes, event and sampling or generation process before interpreting a probability.
A suitable first stopping point is the calculation of P(B∪A)=5/6P(B\cup A)=5/6 at the end of Section 4. Continue to the triplet and axioms once the class can identify the complement event OO. Use Sections 6–8 for another session of numerical recordings, distributions and applications. The technical measure-theoretic development remains in the supplement. Bertrand’s chord problem is posed here but not derived; the rigorous supplement specifies its sampling models and works through their parametrizations and probabilities.

The PMF after the calculation






NoteDefinition: a discrete random variable and its PMF



A random variable is discrete when its values lie in a finite or countably infinite set with probability 1. Its probability mass function is
pX(x)=P(X=x).p_X(x)=P(X=x).
A valid PMF satisfies
pX(x)≥0,∑xpX(x)=1.p_X(x)\ge0,\qquad \sum_x p_X(x)=1.
For a set of values AA,
P(X∈A)=∑x∈ApX(x).P(X\in A)=\sum_{x\in A}p_X(x).


The sum runs over possible values; values outside the stated range have mass zero. For the support example, the masses sum to 0.4+0.3+0.2+0.1=10.4+0.3+0.2+0.1=1. The distribution describes uniform selection from these fixed records. A forecast for new cases requires additional assumptions.

In the support audit, equally likely IDs produce unequal PMF masses because different numbers of IDs have each follow-up count. In the supply model, the elementary states already have unequal weights, and states with the same count have their weights added. In both cases,
P(X=x)=∑ω:X(ω)=xP({ω})P(X=x)=\sum_{\omega:X(\omega)=x}P(\{\omega\})

Worked example 2: accounting discrepancy counts
Select one of twelve invoice IDs uniformly. Seven have no recorded discrepancy, three have one, and two have two. Let DD count discrepancies. Then
pD(0)=712,pD(1)=312,pD(2)=212.p_D(0)=\frac7{12},\qquad p_D(1)=\frac3{12},\qquad p_D(2)=\frac2{12}.
The probability of at least one discrepancy is
P(D≥1)=312+212=1−712=512.P(D\ge1)=\frac3{12}+\frac2{12}=1-\frac7{12}=\frac5{12}.
There are seven discrepancy instances across the twelve invoices: three on the one-discrepancy invoices and four on the two-discrepancy invoices. Selecting an invoice uniformly is a different experiment from selecting one of those seven instances uniformly. State the sampling unit before choosing the denominator.


Worked example 2a: financial loss records
Select one of eight fixed insurance-claim IDs uniformly. Four have recorded loss ₹0, three have ₹50, and one has ₹200. Let LL record the loss. The PMF is pL(0)=4/8p_L(0)=4/8, pL(50)=3/8p_L(50)=3/8 and pL(200)=1/8p_L(200)=1/8, with zero mass elsewhere. Consequently P(L>50)=1/8P(L>50)=1/8, whereas P(L≥50)=4/8P(L\ge50)=4/8. The currency values are the random-variable values; the fractions are their probabilities. This is selection from fixed records, not a forecast of future losses.


Worked example 3: a countably infinite PMF
For a stipulated IT retry model, let NN be the number of failures before the first successful attempt, with
pN(n)=34(14)n,n=0,1,2,….p_N(n)=\frac34\left(\frac14\right)^n,\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.
This model corresponds to independent attempts with success probability 3/43/4 on every attempt, continued until success. Here independence means that learning the outcomes of earlier attempts does not change the stipulated success probability of the next attempt. Section 7 gives the formal independence condition. There is no fixed maximum count. The geometric-series identity verifies the PMF:
∑n=0∞pN(n)=3411−1/4=1.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}p_N(n)=\frac34\frac1{1-1/4}=1.
At least two failures before success has probability
P(N≥2)=1−pN(0)−pN(1)=1−34−316=116.P(N\ge2)=1-p_N(0)-p_N(1)
=1-\frac34-\frac3{16}=\frac1{16}.
Actual retries may have changing success chances or a retry limit; those require a different model. The example shows that “discrete” does not mean “only finitely many values.”

2. Accumulated probability: the CDF

Worked example 4: a follow-up threshold
Return to XX in Example 1. A manager asks for the probability that the follow-up count is at most a chosen threshold. For thresholds 0, 1 and 2 the answers are 0.40.4, 0.70.7 and 0.90.9.
The cumulative distribution function of any real-valued random variable is
FX(x)=P(X≤x).F_X(x)=P(X\le x).
Here it is the step function
FX(x)={0,x<0,0.4,0≤x<1,0.7,1≤x<2,0.9,2≤x<3,1,x≥3.F_X(x)=\begin{cases}
0,&x<0,\\
0.4,&0\le x<1,\\
0.7,&1\le x<2,\\
0.9,&2\le x<3,\\
1,&x\ge3.
\end{cases}
For example, FX(1.5)=0.7F_X(1.5)=0.7: counts 0 and 1 are included. The jump at 2 is 0.20.2, the probability of exactly two follow-ups. The CDF is nondecreasing, right-continuous, and approaches 0 and 1 at the two ends of the real line.
The interval rule is
P(a<X≤b)=FX(b)−FX(a),a<b.P(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a),\qquad a<b.
Consequently P(1<X≤3)=1−0.7=0.3P(1<X\le3)=1-0.7=0.3. Including 1 changes the answer: P(1≤X≤3)=0.3+0.2+0.1=0.6P(1\le X\le3)=0.3+0.2+0.1=0.6. At a value carrying positive probability, endpoint wording matters.
Stopping point 1. Work several PMF and CDF questions before introducing density. Learners should be able to distinguish a possible value from its probability and explain which values a threshold includes.

From counting outcomes to measuring length and area

Worked bridge: uniform grid selection and a uniform location
Divide a rectangular field into 10 rows and 10 columns of equal-area cells. The leftmost four columns are marked for inspection. Select one of the 100 cell IDs uniformly. Forty IDs are marked, so
P(marked cell)=40100=0.4.P(\text{marked cell})=\frac{40}{100}=0.4.
Now describe a different experiment: select a location uniformly by area over the field. The marked region occupies four tenths of the field’s width and its full height. Its area is therefore four tenths of the total, giving
P(marked location)=marked areatotal area=0.4.P(\text{marked location})=\frac{\text{marked area}}{\text{total area}}=0.4.



Equal-area cells connect uniform counting to a uniform area model. The shaded region has probability 0.4 under either stated experiment.


The answers agree because the cells have equal areas and the region is exactly their union. Cell selection produces an ID; location selection produces a point. If cells had unequal areas, uniform selection of their IDs would not be uniform location selection. This is the same distinction as selecting farm plots by ID or by area in Lecture 01.1.






NoteWhat replaces counting in a continuous uniform model?



For equally likely finite outcomes, probability is the fraction of total count:
P(E)=#E#Ω.P(E)=\frac{\#E}{\#\Omega}.
For a uniform location in a finite interval or region, probability is the fraction of total length or area:
P(E)=length⁡(E)length⁡(Ω),P(E)=area⁡(E)area⁡(Ω),P(E)=\frac{\operatorname{length}(E)}{\operatorname{length}(\Omega)},
\qquad
P(E)=\frac{\operatorname{area}(E)}{\operatorname{area}(\Omega)},
respectively, for the ordinary measurable events used here and positive finite total length or area. These are different models sharing the idea of normalizing the appropriate size to total probability 1.
We do not count the individual points in a continuous interval or region. Each point has zero length or area, while an interval or region can have positive size. Countable additivity does not instruct us to sum over uncountably many singleton points.


For a curved marked region, an increasingly fine equal-area grid can approximate its area using the fraction of marked cells. For ordinary regions whose boundaries have area zero, the uncertainty from cells touching the boundary vanishes as the grid is refined. The limiting area is the quantity used in the continuous model; a finite grid remains a discrete approximation.






TipBeyond uniformity: weights become density times width or area



In a discrete model we add probability weights, P(X∈A)=∑x∈ApX(x)P(X\in A)=\sum_{x\in A}p_X(x). In a density model, a small interval near xx has probability approximately fX(x)Δxf_X(x)\,\Delta x when the density varies little across it. Adding these small contributions leads to the integral ∫AfX(x)dx\int_A f_X(x)dx.
For a location in a plane, a small cell contributes approximately fX,Y(x,y)ΔxΔyf_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y. Integrating these contributions gives a region’s probability. Uniform density makes this proportional to geometric area; a varying density gives different weights to equal-area cells.
For example, on the unit interval the uniform density gives P(X≤0.4)=0.4P(X\le0.4)=0.4. Under the stipulated nonuniform density fX(x)=2xf_X(x)=2x on (0,1)(0,1), the same event instead has probability ∫00.42xdx=0.16\int_0^{0.4}2x\,dx=0.16. Its length has not changed; the model’s probability weights have.

3. Continuous measurements: density and area

Worked example 5: voltage tolerance
An electrical measurement model stipulates a voltage error VV uniform on [−0.1,0.1][-0.1,0.1] volts. What is the probability that its absolute error is at most 0.040.04 volts?
The acceptable interval has length 0.080.08 V and the full interval has length 0.20.2 V, giving
P(|V|≤0.04)=0.080.2=0.40.P(|V|\le0.04)=\frac{0.08}{0.2}=0.40.
Its density is
fV(v)={5,−0.1≤v≤0.1,0,otherwise.f_V(v)=\begin{cases}5,&-0.1\le v\le0.1,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
The density height has units V−1^{-1}. Multiplying by interval width gives the probability 5(0.08)=0.405(0.08)=0.40. A density height can exceed 1; the total area must be 1. Here it is 5(0.2)=15(0.2)=1.


The PDF after the calculation






NoteDefinition and interpretation: a probability density function



For the continuous models in this lecture, a probability density function fXf_X is nonnegative and satisfies
∫−∞∞fX(x)dx=1,P(a≤X≤b)=∫abfX(x)dx.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_X(x)\,dx=1,\qquad
P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx.
Probability is area under the density, not its height at a point. In a density model P(X=x)=0P(X=x)=0 for every individual xx, so including or excluding interval endpoints does not change the probability. A rounded measurement is different: a display reading usually represents a small interval of possible underlying values.


In this lecture “continuous” refers to variables described by a density. Mixed distributions and a qualification to this terminology are discussed in the supplement.


Worked example 6: a nonuniform latency density
Suppose request latency TT, measured in seconds, has stipulated density
fT(t)={t/2,0≤t≤2,0,otherwise.f_T(t)=\begin{cases}t/2,&0\le t\le2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
Here tt is the numerical latency in seconds; dimensionally the coefficient 1/21/2 has units s−2^{-2}, so the density has units s−1^{-1}.
First verify the model:
∫02t2dt=[t24]02=1.\int_0^2\frac t2\,dt=\left[\frac{t^2}{4}\right]_0^2=1.
What is the chance of latency exceeding 1 second?
P(T>1)=∫12t2dt=[t24]12=34.P(T>1)=\int_1^2\frac t2\,dt
=\left[\frac{t^2}{4}\right]_1^2=\frac34.
The interval (1,2](1,2] is half the full interval’s length, but contains three quarters of the probability. Ratios of lengths apply to a uniform density, not to every continuous model.
The CDF is
FT(t)={0,t<0,t2/4,0≤t≤2,1,t>2.F_T(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t<0,\\t^2/4,&0\le t\le2,\\1,&t>2.\end{cases}
This follows by integrating from 0 to tt. It also gives P(0.5<T≤1.5)=FT(1.5)−FT(0.5)=(2.25−0.25)/4=1/2P(0.5<T\le1.5)=F_T(1.5)-F_T(0.5)=(2.25-0.25)/4=1/2. For a density model, FT(t)=∫−∞tfT(u)duF_T(t)=\int_{-\infty}^t f_T(u)\,du; where the CDF is differentiable, its derivative gives a version of the density. Here FT′(t)=fT(t)F_T'(t)=f_T(t) except at t=2t=2.


Worked example 7: a rounded display value
In the same model, a system displays latency rounded to the nearest tenth of a second. Ignoring tie endpoints, a displayed value 1.0 represents 0.95≤T<1.050.95\le T<1.05. Thus
P(display=1.0)=1.052−0.9524=0.05.P(\text{display}=1.0)=\frac{1.05^2-0.95^2}{4}=0.05.
This does not conflict with P(T=1)=0P(T=1)=0. The displayed variable is a discrete recording of the continuous latency.

6. Conditionals: restrict the group, then normalize

Worked example 11: pass probability among runs with one retry
In Example 8, six IDs have exactly one retry, and three of those pass. If selection is uniform within those six IDs, the pass probability is 3/6=1/23/6=1/2.
The probability of “one retry and pass” in the full audit is 3/203/20. The probability of selecting the one-retry group is 6/206/20. Their ratio gives
P(Y=1∣X=1)=3/206/20=12.P(Y=1\mid X=1)=\frac{3/20}{6/20}=\frac12.
For events A,BA,B with P(B)>0P(B)>0, conditional probability is
P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)P(B).P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.
The condition changes the group to which probabilities refer. In this example, AA is the pass event and BB is the one-retry event; the numerator counts IDs satisfying both.
The conditional PMF follows:
pY∣X(y∣x)=pX,Y(x,y)pX(x),pX(x)>0.p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)},\qquad p_X(x)>0.
For a fixed xx, its probabilities over yy sum to 1. In this audit the conditional pass probabilities for x=0,1,2x=0,1,2 are 0.8,0.5,0.250.8,0.5,0.25. The conditional fail probabilities are their complements.
Reversing the condition changes the denominator:
P(X=1∣Y=1)=3/2012/20=14.P(X=1\mid Y=1)=\frac{3/20}{12/20}=\frac14.
“One retry among passes” and “pass among one-retry runs” are different questions. Conditioning on an absent group, such as X=3X=3 in this audit, cannot be computed by this ratio because its denominator is zero.


Worked example 12: recovering an overall pass probability
Combine the conditional pass probabilities using the retry-group probabilities:
P(Y=1)=P(Y=1∣X=0)pX(0)+P(Y=1∣X=1)pX(1)+P(Y=1∣X=2)pX(2)=0.8(0.5)+0.5(0.3)+0.25(0.2)=0.60.\begin{aligned}
P(Y=1)&=P(Y=1\mid X=0)p_X(0)\\
&\quad+P(Y=1\mid X=1)p_X(1)+P(Y=1\mid X=2)p_X(2)\\
&=0.8(0.5)+0.5(0.3)+0.25(0.2)=0.60.
\end{aligned}
The unweighted average of the three conditional rates is inappropriate because the groups have unequal sizes. More generally,
pY(y)=∑x:pX(x)>0pY∣X(y∣x)pX(x).p_Y(y)=\sum_{x:p_X(x)>0}p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x).
Equivalently, a joint mass can be reconstructed as pX,Y(x,y)=pY∣X(y∣x)pX(x)p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x). Conditional rates without group weights do not determine the marginal rate.
At the event level the same rearrangement gives P(A∩B)=P(A∣B)P(B)P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B) when P(B)>0P(B)>0. This justifies the ordered-draw rule used in Lecture 01.1: choosing uniformly from nn objects, then uniformly from the remaining n−1n-1, assigns a specified ordered pair probability (1/n)⋅(1/(n−1))(1/n)\cdot(1/(n-1)).


Worked example 13: agricultural condition and germination
Select one of 20 fixed tray IDs uniformly. Twelve trays were labelled adequately watered; nine of these reached the stipulated germination target. Of eight trays labelled dry, two reached it.
The probability of reaching the target given the adequate-water label is 9/12=3/49/12=3/4. Given the dry label it is 2/8=1/42/8=1/4. The overall probability is
34⋅1220+14⋅820=1120.\frac34\cdot\frac{12}{20}+\frac14\cdot\frac8{20}=\frac{11}{20}.
Among the 11 trays reaching the target, the probability of the adequate-water label is instead 9/119/11. Writing AA for adequate water and HH for reaching the target, this reversal is an application of Bayes’ rule:
P(A∣H)=P(H∣A)P(A)P(H)=(3/4)⋅(12/20)11/20=911.P(A\mid H)=\frac{P(H\mid A)P(A)}{P(H)}
=\frac{(3/4)\cdot(12/20)}{11/20}=\frac9{11}.
This calculation describes the given records; it does not isolate the causal effect of watering from seed type or other differences.

7. Independence is a property to check

Worked example 14: do retries and the result behave independently?
In Example 8, the overall pass probability is 0.600.60, but the pass probability given zero retries is 0.800.80. Knowing the retry count changes the distribution of the result. They are not independent under this audit-selection model.
Two events A,BA,B are independent if P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B). For example, in the audit the events “zero retries” and “pass” have intersection probability 0.400.40, rather than 0.50⋅0.600.50\cdot0.60, so those events are dependent.
For discrete variables, independence means
pX,Y(x,y)=pX(x)pY(y)for every pair (x,y).p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)\quad\text{for every pair }(x,y).
One mismatch disproves it: pX,Y(0,1)=0.40p_{X,Y}(0,1)=0.40, whereas pX(0)pY(1)=0.50(0.60)=0.30p_X(0)p_Y(1)=0.50(0.60)=0.30. To establish independence, the factorization must hold for every pair, including pairs with zero mass. In Example 10, Model A factors for every cell; Model B does not.
Stopping point 2. Before moving to two-dimensional densities, work with the count table until joint, marginal and conditional questions lead to the correct cells and denominators.

8. A joint PDF: two continuous measurements

Worked example 15: two sensor errors
Let U,VU,V be the errors of two sensors in a stipulated model that is uniform over the square −1≤u≤1-1\le u\le1, −1≤v≤1-1\le v\le1, with errors in mm. The square has area 4 mm2^2, so its constant joint density is 1/41/4 mm−2^{-2}.
Both sensors being within 0.50.5 mm means (U,V)∈[−0.5,0.5]2(U,V)\in[-0.5,0.5]^2. This smaller square has area 1 mm2^2, hence
P(|U|≤0.5,|V|≤0.5)=14(1)=14.P(|U|\le0.5,|V|\le0.5)=\frac14(1)=\frac14.
A joint PDF fU,Vf_{U,V} is nonnegative, integrates to 1 over the plane, and gives probabilities by integrating over the requested region AA:
P((U,V)∈A)=∬AfU,V(u,v)dudv.P((U,V)\in A)=\iint_A f_{U,V}(u,v)\,du\,dv.
For this model the density is 1/41/4 inside the square and zero outside. Probability comes from density multiplied by area, not from a point value of the density. The region on which a model can place probability is its support; always state it together with the formula.


Worked example 16: an elapsed time inside a total duration
A hypothetical maintenance task has normalized total duration XX and an intermediate inspection time YY, both measured from the task’s start. Stipulate the joint PDF
fX,Y(x,y)={2,0<y<x<1,0,otherwise.f_{X,Y}(x,y)=\begin{cases}2,&0<y<x<1,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
The triangular support expresses that the inspection happens before completion. The time scale is one chosen reference duration; X,YX,Y are dimensionless fractions. A physical task is not automatically uniform on this triangle: uniformity is the model assumption.
The triangle has area 1/21/2, so total probability is 2(1/2)=12(1/2)=1. Written as an integral,
∫01∫0x2dydx=∫012xdx=1.\int_0^1\int_0^x2\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1 2x\,dx=1.
What is the probability that completion occurs by the halfway point of the reference duration?
P(X≤1/2)=∫01/2∫0x2dydx=∫01/22xdx=14.P(X\le1/2)=\int_0^{1/2}\int_0^x2\,dy\,dx
=\int_0^{1/2}2x\,dx=\frac14.
What is the probability that the inspection occurs in the first half of the task’s own duration?
P(Y<X/2)=∫01∫0x/22dydx=∫01xdx=12.P(Y<X/2)=\int_0^1\int_0^{x/2}2\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1x\,dx=\frac12.
The upper integration limit changes with xx. Replacing this triangle with a rectangle would describe a different model.

9. Marginal and conditional densities

Worked example 17: marginal durations from the triangle
For a fixed total duration xx, the inspection time ranges from 0 to xx. Integrate along that vertical slice:
fX(x)=∫0x2dy=2x,0<x<1.f_X(x)=\int_0^x2\,dy=2x,\qquad 0<x<1.
For a fixed inspection time yy, completion must fall between yy and 1:
fY(y)=∫y12dx=2(1−y),0<y<1.f_Y(y)=\int_y^1 2\,dx=2(1-y),\qquad 0<y<1.
Both densities are zero elsewhere. Each integrates to 1. For example,
P(Y>1/2)=∫1/212(1−y)dy=14.P(Y>1/2)=\int_{1/2}^1 2(1-y)\,dy=\frac14.
In general the marginal densities are
fX(x)=∫−∞∞fX,Y(x,y)dy,fY(y)=∫−∞∞fX,Y(x,y)dx.f_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy,\qquad
f_Y(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx.
The stated support determines where the integrand is nonzero and hence the effective bounds.


Worked example 18: inspection time for a given duration
In the same model, consider tasks with total duration close to x=0.8x=0.8. The allowable inspection times occupy 0<y<0.80<y<0.8, and the joint density is constant along the slice. Normalizing that slice gives density 1/0.81/0.8 on this interval. Therefore the model’s conditional probability of inspection before 0.2 is
P(Y<0.2∣X=0.8)=∫00.210.8dy=14.P(Y<0.2\mid X=0.8)=\int_0^{0.2}\frac1{0.8}\,dy=\frac14.
The general conditional density formula is
fY∣X(y∣x)=fX,Y(x,y)fX(x),fX(x)>0.f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)},\qquad f_X(x)>0.
For the triangular model it is 1/x1/x on 0<y<x0<y<x and zero otherwise. For each fixed 0<x<10<x<1, its integral over yy is 1. A conditional probability is found by integrating it over the requested range of yy.
Since XX has a density, P(X=0.8)=0P(X=0.8)=0. This formula is not the elementary event ratio with P(X=0.8)P(X=0.8) in the denominator. For this regular density model it describes the limiting distribution in increasingly narrow duration bands around 0.8. The supplement gives the precise qualification. If a duration is rounded or measured over a band, condition on that band instead.


Worked example 19: conditioning on a band
Using the same triangular model, find P(Y<0.2∣0.6<X<0.8)P(Y<0.2\mid0.6<X<0.8).
The conditioning event has probability
P(0.6<X<0.8)=∫0.60.82xdx=0.82−0.62=0.28.P(0.6<X<0.8)=\int_{0.6}^{0.8}2x\,dx=0.8^2-0.6^2=0.28.
Throughout the band, x>0.6>0.2x>0.6>0.2, so every 0<y<0.20<y<0.2 lies inside the triangular support. The joint event has probability
P(Y<0.2,0.6<X<0.8)=∫0.60.8∫00.22dydx=0.08.P(Y<0.2,0.6<X<0.8)=\int_{0.6}^{0.8}\int_0^{0.2}2\,dy\,dx=0.08.
Their ratio is 0.08/0.28=2/70.08/0.28=2/7. This is an ordinary conditional-event calculation with a positive denominator. It answers a different question from conditioning on X=0.8X=0.8.


Worked example 20: continuous independence
The sensor-square model in Example 15 has fU(u)=1/2f_U(u)=1/2 and fV(v)=1/2f_V(v)=1/2 on (−1,1)(-1,1), and the joint density equals their product. These two errors are independent in the stipulated model.
For variables with a joint PDF, independence is equivalent to
fX,Y(x,y)=fX(x)fY(y)f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)
apart from sets of area zero. Is it true for the maintenance triangle? No: P(Y>X)=0P(Y>X)=0 under the joint model, while independent draws from the two marginals would allow such pairs. For example, on the rectangle 0.1<x<0.20.1<x<0.2, 0.8<y<0.90.8<y<0.9, the joint density is zero and both marginal densities are positive. The triangular support carries dependence even though the density is constant within it.

11. Independent exercises
State the sampling mechanism or density, the variable and the event in every answer. All application scenarios are hypothetical. These questions have no solutions in the student notes or supplement.

Discrete variables and the CDF
D1. Two fair dice. Roll independent fair red and blue dice. Let SS be their total. Construct the PMF, find P(S≥9)P(S\ge9), and find FS(7)F_S(7). Explain why totals are not equally likely.
D2. Financial loss records. Select one of ten loan IDs uniformly. Six have recorded loss ₹0, three have ₹300, and one has ₹1200. Construct the loss PMF and CDF. Find the probabilities of loss strictly greater than ₹300 and loss at least ₹300.
D3. Normalization. A count random variable KK has proposed PMF pK(k)=c(k+1)p_K(k)=c(k+1) for k=0,1,2,3k=0,1,2,3, and zero otherwise. Find cc, P(K≥2)P(K\ge2) and FK(1.5)F_K(1.5).

The counts for (A,R)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)(A,R)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1) are 10,4,2,410,4,2,4. Construct the joint PMF and both marginals. Find P(A=1∣R=1)P(A=1\mid R=1) and P(R=1∣A=1)P(R=1\mid A=1). 1. Outcomes, events and mutual exclusivity
Data Analytics for AI · Executive M.Tech · IIT Jammu
Module 01 · Fundamentals of Probability and Random Signal Theory
Supplement to 01.1 · Introduction to probability through problems
01.1 main materials
Supplementary materials
This supplement gives the formal definitions, parametrizations and derivations supporting the main lecture. Its details are intended for supplementary study alongside the corresponding lecture topics. For the chord calculations, RR is the fixed circle radius, TT the normalized midpoint distance, and LL the chord length, as in the Bertrand deck. The Billing indicator in the main notes remains XBX_B.
The main lecture motivates these constructions with questions about a hypothetical six-ticket routing audit, before introducing the triplet and axioms through finite calculations. The proofs below do not depend on that application; they state the general hypotheses needed for the results.
Reference: Krishna Jagannathan, Probability Foundations for Electrical Engineers, 9 July 2025, Chapters 1, 4 and 11, particularly Definitions 68–70 for measurable functions, random variables and their laws. The calculations of the sampling maps are written out below.
A sample space is required to satisfy two conditions. It must be exhaustive, so that at least one of its elements occurs in any realization of the experiment, and its elements must be mutually exclusive, so that at most one of them occurs. Together these state that exactly one ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega occurs each time the experiment is performed.
Distinct outcomes correspond to disjoint singleton subsets. When these singletons belong to the event collection, they are singleton events:
{ω1}∩{ω2}=⌀whenever ω1≠ω2.\{\omega_1\}\cap\{\omega_2\}=\varnothing\quad\text{whenever }\omega_1\ne\omega_2 .
For countable Ω\Omega the singletons therefore form a countable disjoint partition, Ω=⋃ω∈Ω{ω}\Omega=\bigcup_{\omega\in\Omega}\{\omega\} (a disjoint union).
Outcomes are mutually exclusive; events need not be. For a single roll of a die, Ω={1,2,3,4,5,6}\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}, and the outcomes 22 and 44 cannot both occur. The events
A={2,4,6}(even),B={4,5,6}(greater than 3)A=\{2,4,6\}\ \text{(even)},\qquad B=\{4,5,6\}\ \text{(greater than 3)}
can both occur, since A∩B={4,6}≠⌀A\cap B=\{4,6\}\ne\varnothing.

title: 01.1 supplement · Sets, measurable maps and Bertrand’s paradox
text:
Consequences for calculation
The two cases are handled by different rules, and the distinction above is what separates them.
Because singletons are disjoint, countable additivity applies directly to them, and for a countable event AA whose singletons are measurable
P(A)=∑ω∈AP({ω}).P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}P(\{\omega\}).
For two events no such rule is available, since additivity requires disjointness. The correction term is the shared part:
P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
Writing P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B) for the die events above would count the outcomes 44 and 66 twice.


Two errors that this distinction prevents
A list of events is not a sample space. For one roll of a die, the pair “even” and “greater than 3” is not a sample space: both can occur in a single roll, so the second condition fails. They are events in the finer space {1,…,6}\{1,\ldots,6\}.
A valid sample space need not have equally likely elements. For two independent fair tosses, the list “a head on the first toss”, “a tail then a head”, “two tails” is exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so it is a legitimate sample space. Its members carry probabilities 1/21/2, 1/41/4 and 1/41/4: they group the equally likely ordered outcomes as {HH,HT}\{HH,HT\}, {TH}\{TH\} and {TT}\{TT\}. This calculation also appears in the interpretations deck. Mutual exclusivity is a requirement on the sample space; it says nothing about the probabilities assigned to its elements, and counting the members is valid only when they happen to be equally probable.


The same reading in the Bertrand construction
The sampling procedures in Section 3 produce a geometric chord almost surely. After excluding the stated null cases, we may describe their outputs on the common space 𝒞*\mathcal C_* of nondegenerate, nondiameter chords. In this output description, a chord is an elementary outcome. The three rotationally invariant models use the same chord space and event collection but different probability measures. Their original sampling outcomes can instead be angles, distances or points; Section 3 distinguishes these descriptions.
The event E={c:L(c)>3R}E=\{c:L(c)>\sqrt3R\} is not an outcome. It is a set containing uncountably many chords, and it is assigned a probability as a set.
This last point also marks the limit of the summation rule above. In a continuous model each individual outcome has probability zero, so
∑c∈EP({c})=0≠P(E),\sum_{c\in E}P(\{c\})=0\ne P(E),
and the probability of EE cannot be recovered by adding the probabilities of the outcomes it contains. Countable additivity is additivity over countably many disjoint events, and EE is not a countable union of its singletons. The rule P(A)=∑ω∈AP({ω})P(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}P(\{\omega\}) applies to countable events with measurable singletons; it does not extend to an uncountable event by countable additivity.


Event collections and the probability triplet
The main notes use all subsets as events for finite experiments. Here are the precise requirements for a general triplet (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P).






NoteDefinitions: power set and sigma-algebra



The power set 𝒫(Ω)=2Ω={E:E⊆Ω}\mathcal P(\Omega)=2^\Omega=\{E:E\subseteq\Omega\} contains every subset, including ⌀\varnothing and Ω\Omega. For finite |Ω|=n|\Omega|=n, it has 2n2^n elements, since including or excluding each outcome gives two choices. An event collection ℱ\mathcal F is a subset of 𝒫(Ω)\mathcal P(\Omega), so its members are themselves subsets of Ω\Omega.
The event collection ℱ\mathcal F must be a sigma-algebra on Ω\Omega. Its requirements are:

Contains the sample space: Ω∈ℱ\Omega\in\mathcal F.
Closed under complements: if E∈ℱE\in\mathcal F, then Ec=Ω\E∈ℱE^c=\Omega\setminus E\in\mathcal F.
Closed under countable unions: if E1,E2,…∈ℱE_1,E_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F, then ⋃i=1∞Ei∈ℱ\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}E_i\in\mathcal F.

These conditions ensure that “not EE” and “at least one of E1,E2,…E_1,E_2,\ldots” are events whenever the component sets are events. Since this example has a finite sample space, taking ℱ=2Ω\mathcal F=2^\Omega, the power set, satisfies all three requirements.
No disjointness assumption is needed for closure under unions. It is needed when applying countable additivity of probability. Closure also gives ⌀∈ℱ\varnothing\in\mathcal F, countable intersections by De Morgan’s law, and differences E\F=E∩FcE\setminus F=E\cap F^c.


The probability measure PP is nonnegative, has P(Ω)=1P(\Omega)=1, and is countably additive on pairwise disjoint events. These conditions and the event-collection requirements together define a probability space.
In the six-ticket audit, Ω={t1,…,t6}\Omega=\{t_1,\ldots,t_6\} and B={t1,t2,t5}B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\}.


A smaller event collection
Suppose a dashboard records only whether the selected ticket requires Billing. It distinguishes B={t1,t2,t5}B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\} from Bc={t3,t4,t6}B^c=\{t_3,t_4,t_6\}, but does not identify individual tickets. The events available in this description are
𝒢={⌀,B,Bc,Ω}.\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega\}.
This is a sigma-algebra: complements exchange the pairs, and any union of its members is again one of the four members. Restrict the uniform-ID measure to 𝒢\mathcal G; the four probabilities are 0,1/2,1/2,10,1/2,1/2,1 respectively. The singleton {t1}\{t_1\} is a subset of Ω\Omega but is not an event in 𝒢\mathcal G. The full audit model still uses ℱ=2Ω\mathcal F=2^\Omega; the smaller model illustrates why the event collection must be specified.


A continuous triplet on the unit interval
Suppose a simulation selects a number uniformly from the unit interval. What is the probability that the selected value lies between 1/41/4 and 3/43/4? Uniformity means that an interval’s probability is its length, so the answer should be 3/4−1/4=1/23/4-1/4=1/2. To make this a probability model, we must specify more than intervals: “outside this interval” and “in at least one of these intervals” must also be events.
Take Ωu=[0,1]\Omega_u=[0,1]. A sample point u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] is a number; an event is a suitable set of numbers. We use the Borel σ-algebra
ℱu=ℬ([0,1])=σ({(a,b)∩[0,1]:a,b∈ℝ,a<b}).\mathcal F_u=\mathcal B([0,1])

Here σ(𝒜)\sigma(\mathcal A) means the smallest σ-algebra containing every member of a family 𝒜\mathcal A. Equivalently, it is the intersection of all σ-algebras on [0,1][0,1] that contain that family. Such σ-algebras exist because the power set 2[0,1]2^{[0,1]} is one of them. The intervals intersected with [0,1][0,1] generate all the relatively open sets of the unit interval.
A Borel set is one member of ℬ([0,1])\mathcal B([0,1]). The Borel σ-algebra is the collection of all those members. For example,
[1/4,3/4]∈ℬ([0,1]),[1/4,3/4]⊆[0,1].[1/4,3/4]\in\mathcal B([0,1]),\qquad [1/4,3/4]\subseteq[0,1].
The first statement says it is a measurable event; the second says its elements are possible outcomes.

What the Borel σ-algebra contains
It contains ⌀\varnothing, [0,1][0,1], every relatively open or closed subset, every interval within [0,1][0,1] (including half-open intervals), and every singleton {u}\{u\}. It is closed under complements relative to [0,1][0,1], countable unions and countable intersections. The intersection property follows from De Morgan’s law:
⋂n=1∞En=[0,1]\⋃n=1∞([0,1]\En).\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n

{u}=⋂n=1∞([0,1]∩(u−1/n,u+1/n)).\{u\}=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl([0,1]\cap(u-1/n,u+1/n)\bigr).

These examples do not exhaust the collection: The collection includes sets formed through repeated countable unions, intersections and complements, beyond the examples listed. Closure under countable operations does not imply closure under arbitrary uncountable unions. The Borel σ-algebra is smaller than 2[0,1]2^{[0,1]}; not every subset is Borel. Section 5 below constructs a set that is not Lebesgue measurable. Since every Borel set is Lebesgue measurable, that set is not Borel either.

Here we use the standard theorem that Lebesgue measure exists and is countably additive on Borel sets. Checking a few intervals alone would not establish that theorem. 2. Random variables, inverse images and probability laws
On a probability space (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), a real-valued random variable is a measurable function
X:Ω→ℝ.X:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R.
Measurability means that X−1(B)∈ℱX^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F for every Borel set B∈ℬ(ℝ)B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R). The Borel σ-algebra is generated by open intervals and includes the intervals, singleton sets and their countable combinations used here. For a real-valued function, it is sufficient to check {ω:X(ω)≤x}∈ℱ\{\omega:X(\omega)\le x\}\in\mathcal F for every real xx.

The distinction between a random variable and a set function
A random variable is a function on outcomes, not a real-valued set function on events. It induces the following map between collections of sets:
X−1:ℬ(ℝ)→ℱ,B↦{ω:X(ω)∈B}.X^{-1}:\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\longrightarrow\mathcal F,\qquad
B\longmapsto\{\omega:X(\omega)\in B\}.
The probability measure and the distribution of XX are real-valued set functions:
P:ℱ→[0,1],PX:ℬ(ℝ)→[0,1],P:\mathcal F\to[0,1],\qquad P_X:\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\to[0,1],
PX(B)=P(X−1(B))=P(X∈B).P_X(B)=P\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr)=P(X\in B).
Thus a numerical question about XX is first converted to a set of outcomes, and that event is assigned a probability. This is the set-based construction used in the Bertrand calculation below. It follows the distinction in Jagannathan, Chapter 11, Definitions 68–70.


Independence used in the examples
Events E,FE,F are independent when P(E∩F)=P(E)P(F)P(E\cap F)=P(E)P(F). Random variables U,VU,V are independent when this identity holds for the events {U∈A}\{U\in A\} and {V∈B}\{V\in B\} for every pair of Borel sets A,BA,B. For variables with a joint density on a product domain, fU,V(u,v)=fU(u)fV(v)f_{U,V}(u,v)=f_U(u)f_V(v) almost everywhere implies independence: integrating over A×BA\times B separates into the product of the two marginal integrals. Independent fair tosses below stipulate the product measure, giving each ordered pair mass (1/2)(1/2)=1/4(1/2)(1/2)=1/4.


Worked example: the head count
For two independent fair tosses, each outcome in Ω={HH,HT,TH,TT}\Omega=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\} has probability 1/41/4, and ℱ=2Ω\mathcal F=2^\Omega. Define X(HH)=2X(HH)=2, X(HT)=X(TH)=1X(HT)=X(TH)=1, and X(TT)=0X(TT)=0. Then
PX({1})=P({HT,TH})=1/2,P_X(\{1\})=P(\{HT,TH\})=1/2,
PX([1,2])=P({HH,HT,TH})=3/4.P_X([1,2])=P(\{HH,HT,TH\})=3/4.
The distribution assigns probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/41/4,1/2,1/4 to 0,1,20,1,2. It is obtained through inverse images, not by assuming that the three numerical values are equally likely.


Worked example: an indicator
For an event A∈ℱA\in\mathcal F, its indicator is the random variable
𝟏A(ω)={1,ω∈A,0,ω∉A.\mathbf1_A(\omega)=\begin{cases}1,&\omega\in A,\\0,&\omega\notin A.\end{cases}
Its inverse images satisfy 𝟏A−1({1})=A\mathbf1_A^{-1}(\{1\})=A and 𝟏A−1({0})=Ac\mathbf1_A^{-1}(\{0\})=A^c. Consequently, P(𝟏A=1)=P(A)P(\mathbf1_A=1)=P(A).
For the parity model in the event-collection lab, take 𝒢={⌀,{2,4,6},{1,3,5},Ω}\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\{2,4,6\},\{1,3,5\},\Omega\}. The indicator of an even face is measurable. The numerical face-value function is not measurable relative to that σ-algebra, since the inverse image of {6}\{6\} is the unavailable subset {6}\{6\}.


Measurability and the probability law
Return to the six-ticket audit of Section 1, with B={t1,t2,t5}B=\{t_1,t_2,t_5\}, XB=𝟏BX_B=\mathbf1_B, and 𝒢={⌀,B,Bc,Ω}\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega\}.
To calculate P(XB∈D)P(X_B\in D), the inverse image XB−1(D)X_B^{-1}(D) must be an event. For example, XB−1((1/2,3/2))=B∈ℱX_B^{-1}((1/2,3/2))=B\in\mathcal F, giving probability 1/21/2. This requirement motivates the formal definition.
As with the unit interval in Section 1, now on ℝ\mathbb R, the Borel σ-algebra ℬ(ℝ)\mathcal B(\mathbb R) is the smallest sigma-algebra containing all open intervals. It includes intervals, singletons and their countable unions, intersections and complements. A function X:Ω→ℝX:\Omega\to\mathbb R is measurable, and hence a real-valued random variable on (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal F,P), if
X−1(D)∈ℱfor every D∈ℬ(ℝ).X^{-1}(D)\in\mathcal F\quad\text{for every }D\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).
Its law or distribution is the probability measure
PX(D)=P(X−1(D)),D∈ℬ(ℝ).P_X(D)=P(X^{-1}(D)),\qquad D\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R).
In the full finite model every function is measurable because all subsets are events. For XBX_B, the inverse image is one of ⌀,B,Bc,Ω\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega according to whether DD contains neither of 0 and 1, only 1, only 0, or both. Thus XBX_B is measurable even for the smaller collection 𝒢\mathcal G. Its law assigns mass 1/21/2 each to 0 and 1.
